blocks.text: Artist Keisha Scarville has reworked a childhood passport photograph of her father more than 300 times. Her book Passports explores his past, the link between citizenship and identity, and the Black diaspora.
By Gaia Squarci. Artwork by Keisha Scarville, courtesy of MACK and the artist.

Through images and fragments of text, the book reads like a dialogue with her father: an attempt to understand him better and, through him, to understand her own roots. It begins with a photograph of him at 16, younger than she ever knew him. The images are altered and collaged, multiplying her father’s identity and connecting his story to the histories of the Black diaspora that began centuries before he was born.

Alongside these portraits, archival photographs taken between the 1960s and 1980s in Guyana and New York City evoke the two places that shaped his life: his native Guyana, which he left as a boy, and New York City, where he later settled. A written conversation with her father traces the steps he took, what he gained and lost along the way, and his sense of belonging to a country where he has spent most of his life.
The book Passports is published by MACK and available for £50.00 GBP.
